title: Majestic King
reviewNotes: Three branches, 20 exact positions from the complete seven-piece board. Nb6+ draws out the ...Kc6/...Kb5 counterfork; Bc3 preserves the bishop, and Ke6–d5–c4 builds actual b3 mate despite ...h1=Q. The direct ...Nxb6 Bxb6 ending wins; saving the knight with Nc3+ changes the exact outcome to a draw.
transcript: Fools will resign. Wise players might make a draw, but only a true genius would be able to win from this position. You see, it seems like there's no way to make any progress. The black knight is attacking the last pawn that white has, and the black king is attacking the white knight. But white does have a very precise path to win this position, starting with knight to b6 check. Now, of course, this is a fork. We're attacking the king, and we are trying to dislodge this black knight. If the knight was to take, after the bishop captures the knight, we are now in time to both stop the pawn with bishop to g1 and to run with the king to grab the black pawn and come back to defend our own pawn. But if we go back to that check with the knight, we have to realize that black has another option in the form of king to c6. This seems to make no sense because, of course, now white can pick up the black knight on the edge of the board. Was this just a blunder? Not exactly. Black has king to b5, forking the knight and the bishop. So, we are going to lose one of the two pieces back. Which piece should we save? Interestingly, if we decide to save the knight with knight to c3, this is a blunder. The black king is going to, of course, pick up the bishop, and now the white king is too far to stop the black pawn. So, we are going to need the white knight to run to the other side of the board, and in that time, the black king is going to pick up this pawn. And so, this game is going to end in a draw. So, believe it or not, the only way for white to win this position is to play bishop to c3, saving the bishop and knight to perish. But we need to be careful about how we want to do this. We cannot actually use the bishop to stop the pawn. Now, after king to b3, black is preparing to push the pawn, distract the bishop, and then pick up the white pawn. So, actually, the only winning move for white is to play the very precise and crucial king to e6. This is the only winning move because it's the only plan that is going to allow the king to reach the black pawn. What? How can that be possible? The pawn is running down this side of the board and the king is running to the other side. But you see, if the white king was to chase the pawn, it would have never won the race. The pawn is always one step ahead. So we need to gain one tempo. If at any point the black king decides to move in any way, we are going to gain that crucial tempo that is going to allow us to reach the pawn and win the game. But of course black is under no obligation to move the king. The pawn can simply keep running down the board. But this would be an even greater mistake. After king to c4, black thinks that he's going to win. But he gets it with the cold shower after bishop to b4. This sets up an incredible and unstoppable mating net. Again, black has no other choice but to push the pawn, get the queen, but this is a useless queen because pawn to b3 is going to be a checkmate.
